42874220.label: Purpose
42874220.text: To appraise how periprostatic adipose tissue (PPAT) is defined, sampled, and evaluated in prostate cancer imaging, with emphasis on spatial strategy, intended clinical use, evidence maturity, and imaging-tissue correspondence.

42874220.label: Method
42874220.text: We conducted a structured critical review with evidence mapping, supported by PubMed/MEDLINE and Web of Science searches through August 29, 2026, supplemented by prespecified Google Scholar and citation searches. Two reviewers independently screened records. Reports were mapped by imaging strategy, spatial target, clinical task, evaluation design, reproducibility, cohort overlap, and imaging-tissue correspondence.

42874220.label: Results
42874220.text: The formal evidence set comprised 113 reports, including 63 clinical imaging reports. Strategies comprised morphometry / computed tomography (CT) attenuation (48 reports), tissue-property / compositional imaging (4), PPAT-focused radiomics (4), and interface / multicompartment modelling (7). Quantitative reproducibility was reported in 19/63 clinical reports. Only two reports underwent independent external evaluation, and neither evaluated a PPAT-only model. Biological and translational evidence supported PPAT as a heterogeneous tumour-adjacent compartment, whereas direct spatially matched imaging-tissue validation remained uncommon. Clinical evidence spanned prebiopsy risk refinement, upgrading or active-surveillance reclassification, local extension and surgical planning, prognosis, treatment-related outcomes, and nodal and metastatic assessment; most reports lacked independent evaluation.

42874220.label: Conclusions
42874220.text: PPAT imaging is best regarded as a set of spatially defined, task-specific phenotypes rather than a single biomarker. Current evidence positions PPAT as a candidate adjunct to established clinical and intraprostatic imaging information. Clinical adoption will require reproducible definitions and measurements, task-matched assessment of incremental value, independent external evaluation, and prospective evidence of decision impact.

42951720.label: Background
42951720.text: Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT is increasingly used to evaluate treatment responses in metabolic bone diseases (MBDs), where conventional serum biomarkers and structural imaging fail to show local dynamic changes. The performance and utility of Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in these diseases, however, has not been fully explored. We systematically evaluated the contemporary use of quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT for measuring MBD treatment responses.

42951720.label: Methods
42951720.text: Electronic databases were searched for clinical studies using quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT in MBDs. Risk of bias was assessed via QUADAS-2, ROBINS-I and QUIPS. Results were synthesized narratively.

42951720.label: Results
42951720.text: Thirteen studies (n=14-72 patients; 358 total cases) met inclusion criteria, focusing on chronic kidney disease-mineral and bone disorder (CKD-MBD, n=9 studies) and fibrous dysplasia/McCune-Albright syndrome (FD/MAS, n=4 studies). Two longitudinal studies evaluated therapeutic response: denosumab in FD/MAS yielded comparable reductions in total lesion metabolic activity across moderate (-64.9%) and high doses (-67.0%), while turnover-guided therapy in CKD-MBD significantly reduced bone kinetic flux (Ki). Remaining literature comprised cross-sectional and observational cohorts. Here, PET kinetic (Ki, FUR) and volumetric metrics (TV, TA, TLF) correlated strongly with bone formation rates and circulating biomarkers. Ki and background-adjusted uptake ratios (SUVR) discriminated bone turnover states with high accuracy (ROC AUC up to 0.98), outperforming serum parathyroid hormone in CKD-MBD. Reporting of reconstruction settings was highly variable; only one study explicitly noted EARL scanner accreditation and none documented compliance with EARL Standard 1 or 2. Risk of bias was primarily driven by small cohort sizes, attrition and unadjusted confounding.

42951720.label: Conclusions
42951720.text: Quantitative Na[¹⁸F]F PET/CT provides high diagnostic accuracy for tracking regional turnover and treatment response in benign MBDs. However, clinical adoption is hindered by a lack of harmonized EARL-compliant protocols, unstandardized outcome metrics and a reliance on small, unadjusted cohorts.

42975820.label: Objective
42975820.text: High-energy photons emitted by 123I may penetrate the septa of a collimator, thereby degrading quantitative accuracy. Collimator choice affects the evaluation of the heart-to-mediastinum (H/M) ratio in cardiac sympathetic imaging with 123I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (123I-MIBG). We investigated the validity of previously reported convenient methods for correcting collimator-dependent differences in the H/M ratio.

42975820.label: Methods
42975820.text: Twenty patients who underwent cardiac 123I-MIBG imaging for evaluation of neurodegenerative diseases on a gamma camera system provided by GE Healthcare were studied. Anterior chest images were acquired successively with three collimators: the low-energy high-resolution and sensitivity (LEHRS), extended low-energy general-purpose (ELEGP), and medium-energy general-purpose (MEGP) collimators. The H/M ratios were estimated using various correction methods: 123I-dual-window (IDW) correction using the high-energy subwindow, empiric correction based on 123I point-source imaging, combined correction using the high-energy subwindow and point-source imaging, and phantom-based method using imaging of a dedicated phantom. Empiric correction and combined correction had been established using patient data mainly obtained with a system provided by Siemens Healthineers.

42975820.label: Results
42975820.text: The uncorrected H/M ratios obtained with the LEHRS collimator correlated closely with those obtained with the MEGP collimator but were substantially smaller, indicating severe underestimation with the LEHRS collimator, attributable to septal penetration. The underestimation remained but decreased after any correction. The H/M ratios after correction were largest with combined correction, followed by empiric correction, phantom-based correction, and IDW correction. The absolute errors after correction were smallest for combined correction, followed by empiric correction, phantom-based correction, and IDW correction. The underestimation was substantially smaller with the ELEGP collimator than with the LEHRS collimator, and any type of correction reduced the underestimation.

42975820.label: Conclusions
42975820.text: Convenient correction methods using 123I point-source imaging were valid for reducing collimator-dependent differences in the H/M ratio in cardiac 123I-MIBG imaging, demonstrating their applicability to a GE system.

43002570.label: Background
43002570.text: Quantitative amyloid PET is increasingly used in clinical practice, but the interchangeability of quantification software remains uncertain. We compared quantitative amyloid PET measurements, diagnostic performance, and platform-specific thresholds between two FDA-cleared software packages, MIMneuro and Neurophet SCALE PET, using clinical Florbetapir 18F-PET/CT.

43002570.label: Patients and methods
43002570.text: In this retrospective single-center study, 95 consecutive patients who underwent Florbetapir 18F-PET/CT were independently analyzed using MIMneuro and Neurophet SCALE PET. Quantitative measures included standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) and global Centiloid values. Cross-platform agreement was evaluated using Pearson correlation, Bland-Altman analysis, and Cohen κ statistics. Receiver operating characteristic analysis was used to determine platform-specific thresholds for predicting visual amyloid positivity.

43002570.label: Results
43002570.text: Regional SUVRs showed moderate correlations (r = 0.414 to 0.674; all P < 0.001), with the strongest correlation observed for global Centiloid values (r = 0.684). Neurophet yielded significantly higher global SUVR values than MIMneuro (mean bias, -0.20; P < 0.001), whereas the difference in Centiloid values was not significant. The optimal thresholds for predicting visual amyloid positivity were 1.10 versus 1.40 for global SUVR and 20.7 versus 34.4 for global Centiloids for MIMneuro and Neurophet, respectively. Cross-platform agreement was moderate using SUVR (κ = 0.42) and improved with Centiloids (κ = 0.60).

43002570.label: Conclusions
43002570.text: Although MIMneuro and Neurophet SCALE PET showed moderate agreement, their quantitative measurements were not directly interchangeable at clinically relevant thresholds. These findings suggest that platform-specific quantitative thresholds may be needed when amyloid PET is used for clinical interpretation, longitudinal follow-up, or selection of patients for antiamyloid therapy.

43084070.label: Purpose
43084070.text: This first-in-human study investigated whether scintigraphy with a 99mTc-labelled KN035-derived anti-PD-L1 nanobody could visualise PD-L1-associated uptake in hypofunctional thyroid nodules and whether uptake patterns were related to the predominant PD-L1-positive cell population identified histopathologically.

43084070.label: Methods
43084070.text: Eight patients with scintigraphically hypofunctional thyroid nodules scheduled for thyroidectomy underwent planar scintigraphy and SPECT/CT after intravenous administration of the radiotracer. Tracer uptake was assessed visually and semi-quantitatively using L/T and L/B uptake ratios and was compared with postoperative histopathological findings and qualitative PD-L1 immunohistochemistry.

43084070.label: Results
43084070.text: Tracer administration was well tolerated. Intense focal uptake was observed in oncocytic thyroid tumours with predominant tumour-cell PD-L1 staining, whereas intermediate uptake occurred in lesions with predominant macrophage-like PD-L1-positive cells. Absent or minimal uptake was observed in lesions without identifiable PD-L1 staining. Diffuse thyroid uptake was observed in the patient with Hashimoto thyroiditis, with predominant lymphocyte-like PD-L1-positive inflammatory cells on histopathology. L/T uptake ratios differed across the three predefined histopathological categories (Kruskal-Wallis H = 6.25; P = 0.044), although this exploratory finding requires cautious interpretation given the very small group sizes. No diagnostic threshold or screening algorithm was derived from the observed uptake ratios.

43084070.label: Conclusion
43084070.text: In this exploratory first-in-human study, 99mTc-labelled KN035-derived anti-PD-L1 nanobody scintigraphy was feasible and demonstrated distinct uptake patterns associated with different histopathological PD-L1 staining patterns. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support further prospective investigation of PD-L1-targeted molecular imaging to assess the spatial and cellular distribution of PD-L1 in thyroid tissue.

43096670.text: One-stop catheter ablation (CA) combined with left atrial appendage (LAA) closure (LAAC) is widely used in patients with atrial fibrillation (AFib); however, it is extremely challenging to perform catheter-based procedures in rare cases of AFib with dextrocardia and complex LAA anatomy. Such cases may require precise occlusion strategies, such as dual-device "Kissing LAAC." However, to our knowledge, no cases of one-stop CA combined with Kissing LAAC in patients with AFib, dextrocardia, and complex LAA anatomy have been reported. A 67-year-old woman with persistent AFib and dextrocardia was found on preoperative computed tomography angiography (CTA) to have a complex bilobed LAA with a shared orifice diameter of approximately 26 mm and shared depth of approximately 12 mm. Therefore, single-device closure was considered unlikely to achieve effective occlusion. A one-stop CA combined with LAAC procedure was planned. After CA, intraoperative multi-projection digital subtraction angiography (DSA) was used to determine the deployment angle, evaluate the superior and inferior lobes, and guide device selection. Two 20-mm WATCHMAN FLX devices were implanted under DSA guidance, and the procedure was completed without immediate complications. At the 3-month follow-up, the patient maintained sinus rhythm, and CTA showed stable device position without device-related thrombus. However, a residual shunt of 2.92 mm was observed on 3-month CTA. This case suggests that one-stop CA combined with Kissing LAAC may be technically feasible in a highly selected patient with AFib, dextrocardia, and complex bilobed LAA anatomy, and it may provide a valuable clinical reference for similar cases.
